en: A Brief Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty by Imperial Decree Interpreted by the Disciples of the Buddha (Weng Chun and Wang Xiguan)
Commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
As for "Vajra," it is that which is the most refined and solid among gold. It is produced from within gold; even after being smelted a hundred times, it does not diminish.
Sharpness can sever things, just as wisdom can sever all inverted perceptions of greed, anger, and delusion.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *prajñā*, which here means "wisdom. In the Sanskrit language it is called *pāramitā*, which here means "reaching the other shore."
To reach the other shore, one must rely upon wisdom. As for the *sūtra*, this scripture is the path for studying the Buddha.
○ First Division: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly.
This division describes the causes and conditions from which the gathering for the preaching of the Dharma arose. Examining the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is found that...
It consists of six hundred fascicles and comprises sixteen assemblies in total; this [specific assembly] comprises five hundred and seventy-seven fascicles.
It is the ninth assembly at the second location, the Jeta Grove (Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park).

According to the preceding account, when the Buddha was at the Deer Park turning the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, he feared that people might consequently become attached to the notion of marks (*nimitta*). Therefore, during the Prajñāpāramitā assembly, he expounded the markless (*animitta*).
The True School requires that people see their nature and attain Buddhahood; it does not permit even a single thread of attachment toward anything outside the mind.

Therefore, it sweeps away the marks of seeking Buddhahood, sweeps away the marks of grasping at Bodhisattvas, sweeps away the marks of being able to deliver sentient beings, and sweeps away the marks of verbal expressions.
One sweeps away the marks of cultivation, yet simultaneously does not give rise to the mark of annihilation. It is empty yet not empty; it exists yet is not existent.
To perceive the nature as suchness (tathatā)—the great matter of the Dharma assembly culminates herein.
(The Buddha had two great disciples, Ānanda and Kāśyapa, who together recounted this sutra. Their words were as follows: "Thus have I heard from the Buddha at one time.

The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī (the capital of King Prasenajit). Outside the city was the Jeta Grove (a grove donated by Prince Jeta), the park purchased by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada (Sudatta).

Within it a vihāra had been built, where the Buddha was invited to preach the Dharma. He was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand, who had attained profound realization."

Accompanied by two hundred and fifty people, at that time, the Buddha, the Honored One of the World, dressed in his great *saṃghāṭī* robe and carrying the alms bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings, entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food among the households.

Within that city, he did not discriminate between the noble and the lowly, but maintained an impartial view as he went from house to house in succession. Having finished begging for food, he returned to his original location in the garden and [took] what he had received...
Having finished eating, they put away their robes and bowls, washed their feet, and then arranged high seats upon which they sat cross-legged.
(At this point, one may clarify the Way according to the circumstances.
Commentary: When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, Ānanda requested: "What words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?

The Buddha commanded that the four characters "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) be placed there as the opening phrase. "Buddha" is called *bhagavān* in Sanskrit; in the language of Tang, it means...
Awakened. He awakens himself and awakens others, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was an elder named Sudatta, who was so called because he constantly provided for the destitute, the poor, the orphaned, and the solitary. He wished to seek out an excellent site to make offerings to the Buddha.
The Prince Jeta’s park was vast and magnificent. He went there to inquire of the prince, who said in jest, "If you cover the entire park with gold, I shall sell it.
Sudatta then transported gold and spread it across eighty *krośas* of the park until it was completely covered.
The prince would not accept it; thus, they together constructed a vihāra. Therefore, it is collectively known as Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika-ārāma.
"Yuan" (Garden). In Sanskrit, he is called *bhikṣu*; here it is translated as "mendicant. He begs for the Dharma to clarify his own mind, and he begs for food to plant the seeds of merit in others.
Because the Buddha is the Honored One of the three realms, he is titled "World-Honored One" (*Lokanātha*).
The three realms are the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Section Two: The Chapter on the Request of Subhūti.
In this section, Subhūti pays his respects and makes a formal request; all that he asks concerns matters pertaining to the Bodhisattva path.
In the third and fourth [sections], the Buddha likewise answers with matters concerning the Bodhisattva. Thus, it points toward what was asked regarding *samyaksambodhi*.
The mind. Therefore, the seventeen-part question-and-answer remains as before, with the addition of two phrases: "one should give rise to such a mind" and "there is no dharma.
In reality, the phrase "there is no dharma" is used precisely because it is free from the four marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and thus the questions are posed to clarify its subduing [of those marks].
At that time, there was an elder named Subhūti who was among the great assembly.

He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder (to show his readiness to receive and uphold the teaching), knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose myriad dharmas are perfectly integrated—truly a rarity within the triple world!"

Furthermore, by means of the nature of suchness, with clear wisdom penetrating all, they manifest according to where they arise; they are well able to protect and sustain all bodhisattvas who study the Buddha-dharma.

(This shall cause them to believe and accept this Dharma, so that they are not invaded by Māra. You are well able to entrust and consign it to all Bodhisattvas (who study the Buddha), (so that they may practice and uphold this Dharma without interruption at any time.

Such is your compassionate guidance; now I venture to ask the World-Honored One: If there are sons or daughters of good family (who serve the Buddha) who (desire to sever worldly ties and seek to give birth to concentration and wisdom, and thereby) resolve their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should they (properly) abide (in this mind? It lies solely in the true nature.)

[Subhūti asked: "How does one subdue the mind of all delusive thoughts so as not to allow it to shake the true nature? The Buddha [praised him and] said: "Excellent! Excellent! Subhūti, it is just as you have asked.

Indeed, as you have said, the Tathāgata—out of compassion and guidance—skillfully protects and cares for all bodhisattvas [so that evil Māras cannot invade them], and skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas [so that they do not regress]. I shall now expound this vast Dharma. You...
Now listen attentively and receive [this teaching]. I shall explain it to you in detail, just as you have asked.

If there are sons or daughters of good family who can resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment)—those who wish to seek abiding in the true nature—should know that they must abide in this way.

Those who wish to subdue the deluded mind should likewise subdue their minds in this way. (Why? Because when the mind perishes, objects become empty; when objects become empty, the mind is extinguished. [The words were not yet finished.]
Then Subhūti replied: "So be it, so be it, World-Honored One. These words of yours are what my heart desires and delights in; they are what I wish to hear."
Explanation: In Sanskrit he is called Subhūti; here [in Chinese] he is called Śubhamati (Good Auspiciousness), Śubhavyūha (Good Manifestation), or Gaganaprabhava (Born from Space).

When the Venerable One was first born, physiognomists divined his fate and found it to be only auspicious and only good. Later, by interpreting the Dharma of emptiness, he manifested this prior sign. As for "tathā" (如):
The true nature of the Buddha manifests itself with spontaneous ease: through clarity, it illuminates immeasurable worlds; through wisdom, it penetrates the events of immeasurable kalpas.
That which "comes" is the manifestation of True Suchness (Tathatā), appearing and responding in accordance with every situation.
As for the two characters [of the title], they speak of both essence and function: in Sanskrit, *bodhi*, which here means "awakening"; in Sanskrit, *sattva*, which here means "sentient beings."
It is said that this refers to the capacity for awakening within sentient beings. In Sanskrit it is *an*, which here means "non-";
in Sanskrit it is *uttara*, which here means "above"; in Sanskrit it is *sam*, which here means "right"; in Sanskrit it is *yak*, which here means "equal";
and in Sanskrit it is *bodhi*, which here means "awakening. Taken together, it is called "Unsurpassed, Right, Equal, and Perfect Awakening" (*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Section Three: The Orthodox Tradition of the Mahāyāna.
"Mahāyāna" means that it is like a great carriage which carries all things without exception. "Orthodox Tradition" means that it is the legitimate lineage rather than a collateral branch.
While Subhūti spoke of both "abiding securely" and "subduing," here we designate only "subduing."
Why is this? It is because one who wishes to abide in the true mind must first subdue the deluded mind.
While it is relatively easy to move toward stillness, if one proceeds toward the salvation of sentient beings, the mind encounters its objects.

Should the subduing of the deluded mind be even slightly ineffective, the subtle ignorance within will stir from its hidden state, and one will immediately depart from true permanence; thus, one cannot be said to "abide."
The Buddha (calling out to him) said to him: "Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to seek abiding securely in this mind must first subdue their deluded minds."

One should thus subdue the mind (neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil). When the mind ceases and objects cease—just as I deliver sentient beings—how could one possibly cling to even a speck of dust-like appearance?
Among all classes of sentient beings in the world, there are nine types:

those born from eggs (who create karma through deluded nature), those born from wombs (who transmigrate through habituated nature), those born from moisture (who coalesce through baleful vapors), and those born by transformation (who manifest through sensory contact). These...

These four types are all sentient beings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); apart from these, there are devas and humans. If one discriminates between right and wrong without yet realizing the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), yet possesses a physical body (*rūpakāya*) without the forms of male or female and has already severed sensual desires—this is called the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

If one clings to the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) and does not cultivate merit or wisdom, possessing only a conscious spirit while entirely lacking a physical body—this is called the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

If one speaks of the Buddha-dharma with the mouth but does not act according to it, remaining in tranquil non-action while merely maintaining conceptual thoughts—these two [types] are both called the formless realm. As for those without thought (*asaṃjñin*), they sit in meditation to eliminate delusions and possess no active functioning.

As for those in the Realm of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (neither having perception nor lacking it): because they do not cling to the perception of dualistic phenomena, it is called "not having"; because the mind seeking the principle remains present, it is called "not lacking.

This is the highest among all the heavens of the triple world, and their lifespan is the longest, exceeding eighty thousand kalpas. All of these possess the wondrous mind that is neither born nor extinguished, relying on the power of the Buddha-dharma.

I shall cause them all to awaken to and enter the meaning of perfect purity—without a single remaining trace of habitual tendencies, afflictions, forms, or consciousness—reaching the state of non-arising, which is called *nir* (non-birth), and the state of non-death, which is called *vāṇa* (cessation). Thus, one exhausts the burden of undergoing births throughout successive kalpas.

Thus they are extinguished and purified. Having crossed over and been liberated from the ocean of birth-and-death suffering, one arrives at this point where the Buddha and sentient beings’ original nature are as they are, and together ascend to the other shore.
Yet, although sentient beings possess this original nature, they cannot liberate themselves; they must now rely entirely upon the power of the Way to achieve awakening.

When it comes to thus extinguishing and delivering immeasurable, countless, and boundless sentient beings—though this may seem many—in reality, sentient beings clarify themselves and their original nature liberates itself. The ocean of suffering and the Buddha-dharma have never existed; nothing has been added to them. Fundamentally, there are no sentient beings.

Those who have attained extinction (nirvāṇa) by birth—why is this so? It is because the Buddha-mind is universally equal; it does not differentiate sentient beings according to their physical forms or characteristics. Subhūti, [it is for this reason].

If a bodhisattva possesses a mind of subject and object, and treats sentient beings with contempt, this is the mark of self (*ātman*). To take pride in one's own observance of the precepts while looking down upon those who break them is the mark of person (*pudgala*).

To loathe the sufferings of the three miserable realms and aspire to be born among the devas is the mark of sentient being (*sattva*). To cherish long life in one's heart, diligently cultivate meritorious deeds, and cling to dharmas without forgetting them is the mark of life-span (*jīva*).

Thus, one has already fallen into the four evil karmas of greed, anger, delusion, and attachment. Where there is a mark, there is a sentient being; where there is no mark, there is a Buddha. One should simply not regard the deliverance of sentient beings as a personal achievement, but realize that nothing is attained, because the four marks have been completely eliminated. Suppose...

If one gives rise to the thought of being able to deliver sentient beings, this is the view of a self among sentient beings; such a person is not a bodhisattva. This very mind of signlessness is precisely the method for subduing the deluded mind.
Commentary: In the language of Śakya, he is called a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva; here it means "one who awakens sentient beings. *Mahā* means "great.
Section Four: The Non-Abiding of Sublime Practice.
The Emperor asked, "How does one abide? This answer—that there is no abiding—what does it mean? "Constant abiding" refers to the essence (*tattva*);

"non-abiding" refers to the function (*vṛtti*). Abiding within non-abiding is called true abiding. Furthermore, the statement "abide as instructed" answers the intent of abiding in tranquility and subduing [the mind].
(The two great disciples) again [recounted] the sequence [of the Buddha’s words]. The Buddha called them once more and addressed them, saying:
“Subhūti, regarding this Dharma, a bodhisattva must not have any place of dwelling or attachment. With this mind that is free from dwelling and attachment, one should practice the act of giving.

This is what is meant by giving without dwelling upon or attaching to the objects of form (rūpa), without dwelling upon sounds (śabda), odors (gandha), tastes (rasa), tangibles (spraṣṭavya), or mental phenomena (dharma).”
Subhūti, [if one] practices giving with the hope of obtaining something from the various sense objects (dharmas), [then] what connection does such giving have with my original nature?

The Bodhisattva, having received the Tathāgata’s teaching on signlessness, benefits all sentient beings solely through the gift of Dharma. One should give in this manner: [with] both object and self empty, not dwelling upon or clinging to signs. Why is this?

Because when ordinary people practice giving, they do so merely to satisfy their desires; first they bestow wealth upon others, and later they seek merit for themselves. Since the wealth bestowed is finite, the merit obtained—[likewise]—is limited.

There is also an end. If a Bodhisattva, with a pure single mind, benefits all beings, and does not dwell upon or cling to forms—seeing no "I" within who is able to give, and seeing no "I" without who receives the gift—and thus practices giving that fills all of space, then this merit is truly (incalculable and beyond measure.

Subhūti, (I say that the merit of a Bodhisattva is immeasurable; what do you think? For the Bodhisattva does not cling to forms, and their Dharma-giving is vast, encompassing all things in the world without exception. Now, let us examine this:)
"Can the eastern void be measured (or exhausted)? Subhūti replied: 'No, can the void be measured to its end?'"

"It is indeed as the World-Honored One has said. The Buddha spoke again: "Subhūti, [it is likewise] in the south, west, and north, as well as in the four intermediate directions, from above reaching to heaven and below reaching to earth."
"Can that space (the locus of emptiness) be measured (exhausted by calculation)? Subhūti replied: 'No, can one exhaust space by means of calculation? "No."

"It is indeed as the World-Honored One has said. The Buddha then addressed him, saying: "Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling upon or becoming attached to signs, the merit they thereby receive is likewise immeasurable, like the empty space of the ten directions.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva now wishes to receive the Tathāgata’s teaching and abide in the sublime Dharma of the mind, they should simply rely on these words of 'non-abiding. They should dwell according to what has been taught; this alone is truly abiding in the true nature of reality. For there is no [true] abiding..."

All attachments are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). That which is without dwelling or attachment is the place where the fundamental mind abides; therefore, non-dwelling is itself dwelling, and this is true dwelling.
Commentary: The "Dharma of touching phenomena" does not refer to the Buddha-dharma; it is merely the magical art of conceptualization within the minds of ordinary people.
Section Five: Seeing According to Reality as It Is.
"Tathā" (如) is equivalent to the common expression "sovereign" (自在). The essence of its nature is eternally sovereign and entirely devoid of further change;
this constitutes the principle of true nature. Therefore, it is called "the principle as it is" (如理).

Ordinary people are unable to recognize or adhere to this "principle as it is," because they perceive only illusory forms and cast their true, real original nature behind their heads. Thus, they proceed to perceive the Tathāgata [in that manner].
"What connection do the thirty-two marks have with my true nature? (The Buddha called again: "Subhūti, (wishing to clarify the markless true nature,) what do you think? (I shall ask you:

since you, the Tathāgata, possess the full Buddha-nature and also possess the Buddha-body,) can one (by means of the thirty-two kinds of adorned) bodily marks (—that is to say, by this very thing—) see the Tathāgata? (Subhūti replied: "If one merely sees the bodily marks of the Tathāgata, how could that [be sufficient]?"

[One] would thus see the Tathāgata. “No, World-Honored One. (For the Tathāgata does not originally manifest within physical characteristics; he) cannot be seen as a Tathāgata by means of physical characteristics. Why is this?
The physical characteristics spoken of by the Tathāgata (are not originally form or color; they are the Dharma-body within empty space).
They are therefore not (substantially existent) physical characteristics (that can be seen). The Buddha again addressed Subhūti, saying: “Whatever [exists] in the world—all of it...”

All physical forms and characteristics—though they possess such bodies and appearances, they lack any true, substantial nature. In an instant, they are digested and return to emptiness; how could they not all be illusory?

If one can recognize this principle, then seeing that all physical forms and characteristics are not real characteristics, the true reality of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body will immediately manifest before one. Thus, one sees the Tathāgata.
To discern the Dharma-body within the physical body is because the Tathāgata originally exists within one's own self-nature.
Commentary: The Prince’s name was Siddhārtha, which in the Han language means "Sudden Auspiciousness.
At the time of his birth, he possessed the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, emitting a great radiance that universally illuminated the trichiliocosm.
Chapter Six: The Rarity of Right Faith.
This chapter explains how a person, with a mind of right faith, accepts [the teaching] while completely relinquishing all forms and signs; this is truly rare.
Previously, when Śūnyatā-utpanna first clung to the existence of marks (*nimitta*), the Buddha refuted this by means of non-abiding in marks.
Later, he doubted the absence of marks because he could not realize the fruit that possesses marks; thus, he clung to the Buddha as having marks.

The Buddha refuted this by means of the Dharma-body being non-marked, so that through the cause of non-markedness one may realize the fruit of non-markedness. Are not both cause and fruit then empty? Thus, person and dharma are both transcended.
"Extinction. This meaning is profoundly deep and extremely difficult to believe and understand; thus, one doubts and asks the Buddha, and so forth.
It is because the minds and thoughts of sentient beings are stirred that, as soon as there is grasping or attachment, one enters into what is not the Dharma.
Truly, if one causes these thoughts and emotions to be forgotten and wisdom to open, thereby subduing the mind and abiding in peace, one will directly and immediately attain the truth.
Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, in this world today, many are deluded and few have attained awakening.

Amidst such widespread confusion, is there perhaps any sentient being who, upon hearing even a single chapter or a single phrase of such words as these from me, the Buddha, gives rise to true faith and attains immediate and complete understanding?
The Buddha told Subhūti: "The Tathāgata takes the liberation of sentient beings as his heart's purpose and deeply wishes that they hear and accept my words. You must not harbor such doubts."
...this is the teaching. After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, five hundred years later, there will be those who uphold the precepts and commit no evil deeds.

Those who cultivate merit (and practice all manner of goodness) will be able to give rise to a mind of faith and acceptance toward the general meaning of this chapter and the explanation of its individual phrases.

Taking this as true and free from doubt, one should know that such a person (who possesses this faith) will deliver themselves and others, benefiting beings boundlessly in the future until they attain Buddhahood.
It is not merely under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas that they have planted roots of goodness;

rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas, causing their faith to be non-dual [in all of them]. Thus it is evident that these sentient beings have heard...
Regarding these phrases, Subhūti, even those who give rise to a single thought of pure faith—cleansing the dust and severing defilement—the Tathāgata fully knows them and fully sees them.

These sentient beings who possess such faith shall obtain immeasurable merit and virtue as the fruit thereof. Why is this? It is because these sentient beings have heard the wondrous Dharma of the Buddha.

The fundamental nature is perfectly luminous, and all forms and appearances are completely transformed. There is no longer the mark of a self (*ātman*) that clings to fixedness; the mark of a person (*pudgala*) characterized by dualistic opposition;

the mark of a sentient being (*sattva*) characterized by aversion to suffering; or the mark of a life-sustainer (*jīva*) characterized by craving and attachment. Furthermore, there is no mark of relying on the Buddha’s Dharma through intellectual consciousness, nor is there any mark of rejecting the Buddha’s Dharma to cling stubbornly to empty stillness.
When all such marks are utterly abandoned, this is called pure faith. It must be signless (*animitta*) to be truly immeasurable. Why is this so? It is because these sentient beings, if...

If one grasps at signs of form within the mind, this constitutes being attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. How could one’s true nature then be perfectly fulfilled everywhere?

If one grasps at signs of phenomena within the mind, this likewise constitutes being attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. How could one then realize the unconditioned sovereignty of true nature?

For what reason is this? It is because the true nature (*dharmatā*) fundamentally admits not even a hair’s breadth of attachment. How much more so is this the case when one takes up the marks of "existence" or "non-dharma" within the mind;

such acts likewise involve attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. How could this possibly allow the true nature to be empty and luminous, manifesting through skillful means (*upāya*)?

For this very reason, one should not grasp at dharmas—lest there be attachment to existence—and one should not grasp at non-dharmas—lest there be attachment to emptiness. In sum, it is because there is no [duality] that there is no excellence.

...the meaning of characteristics (lakṣaṇa). (Originally there is nothing to which one can cling. For this reason alone. Consider how the Tathāgata, in delivering sentient beings, constantly says to you bhikṣus who study the Buddha’s path:

"You must know the Dharma I have taught. When the nature [of phenomena] is not yet understood, words cannot be dispensed with—just as when one has not yet crossed a river, a raft cannot be dispensed with.

Yet once one has crossed, it is abandoned. Using the raft as a metaphor, even the Buddha's Dharma should be relinquished once one reaches the other shore; how much more so that which is not the Buddha's true Dharma? [Thus, one gives rise to pure faith in reality.]
One should directly perceive one's own nature (xing) and not allow oneself to be obstructed by various conditions.

Commentary: "One who has faith" means believing that the Prajñāpāramitā can eliminate all afflictions, can bring to fruition all supramundane merits, and can give birth to all Buddhas; it also means believing in the Buddha-nature within one's own body.
It is originally pure and free from defilement, non-dual with the Buddha.
To believe that the sentient beings of the six realms are originally without marks, and to believe that all sentient beings will fully attain Buddhahood—this is called pure faith.
Chapter Seven: Neither Attainment nor Exposition.
True nature is empty and quiescent; it possesses no form or appearance. If a person can awaken to the emptiness of nature, then what concern have the Buddha-dharma and I?
What, indeed, could one obtain? All that the Buddha has spoken is merely a provisional means to guide the deluded and lead them toward enlightenment.
Upon reaching the ultimate true nature, all words and speech are entirely inapplicable; yet, what else could be said? This is the simultaneous negation of both Buddha-dharma and views.
The four characters "there is no fixed dharma" (*wú yǒu dìng fǎ*) within the text are precisely the "eye of the school.
Not only do they serve as a pointing-out for Subhūti, but the three characters "unconditioned dharma" (*wéifǎ*) are identical [in their function].

"If even dharmas should be relinquished, where then will the Buddha be? Subhūti, regarding the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, do you know what it is? The Tathāgata’s unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is fundamentally empty and quiescent;

how could there be anything else to be attained apart from the mind? If one were to point to this awakened nature as something possessed exclusively by the Tathāgata, would the Tathāgata truly have an "unexcelled, perfect enlightenment" that he alone has attained?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has extensively taught this perfect enlightenment for the sake of others; thus, the Dharma of the Tathāgata resides directly within words.
[The Buddha asked: "Have you seen that the Tathāgata has ever preached any Dharma? Subhūti replied:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed dharma whatsoever [to be found] within the profound and wondrous, ineffable, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment realized by those who enter it."
This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Yet, in truth, there is nothing for the Tathāgata to attain.

Out of compassion for sentient beings who are mired in delusion, the Tathāgata guides them toward the true nature through expedient means—what is known as "prescribing medicine according to the illness. It should be seen that there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach. Why is this?

Since dharmas are not fixed, how could those who hear the Dharma cling to them as being fixed? One must know that all the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are to be cultivated through the [inherent] nature. None of them...

It can be grasped through the marks of form; it can be transmitted through the mind. Yet, it cannot be sought through words or speech. One must awaken and understand it for oneself alone before it is attained.

For the Dharma is originally no-dharma—this is called "not-dharma. Furthermore, seeing one's nature does not depart from the Dharma—this is called "not-not-dharma. When both having dharma and having no dharma are seen to be incorrect, and one finds the single point of correctness from this, only then is it the true Dharma.

Why is it that those who study the Buddha cannot immediately see the Tathāgata? It is simply because all the worthy and holy ones of every practice take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Dharma of true nature as their foundation.

(To provide proof for the preceding [section]: although there are differences—due to the varying depths of one's faculties and the partiality or correctness of one's intellectual understanding, where even a hair’s breadth of deviation leads to a distance of a thousand li)—there are distinctions (of equal parts). (They cannot be made uniform and identical with the Tathāgata’s same essence.
This is how Śūnyatā-utpanna deeply accords with the principle of formlessness.)

Commentary: Whether it be observing the precepts and practicing patience, or exerting oneself in vigor and meditative concentration, or gathering sand to build stupas and prostrating, or reciting the name "Namo Buddha"—these practices vary according to what individuals cultivate; there is no fixed rule.
[The teaching] may be expounded for those who aspire to the supreme Dharma, or for those who seek unsurpassed wisdom, or for those who seek the state of a Śrāvaka, or for...
The teaching for those seeking Pratyekabuddhahood is to respond according to the individual's capacity;
thus, there is no fixed dharma. Section Eight: Arising from the Dharma.
